 BOISE — Idaho has broken its record in grocery tax refunds, returning $254 million to Idahoans through the 2025 credit.
 Gov. Brad Little announced the record-setting return on Friday, which marks the largest refund in state history, beating the prior year’s mark by $49 million. The number still has room to climb as the Idaho State Tax Commission processes its final claims for the tax year.
 "We know high grocery prices are squeezing family budgets and hitting our seniors hard. That’s exactly why the Legislature and I have focused on giving back more in tax relief,” Little said in a release from his office. “We are committed to making Idaho more affordable, and this record-breaking food tax relief is proof that we’re committed to keeping more of your money where it belongs — in your wallet.”
 To this point, the Tax Commission has processed 813,241 food tax credit claims for 2025 totaling $254,849,965. In 2024, Idaho issued $205,162,246 in returns across 822,401 claims and $201,902,723 in returns across 805,341 in claims for 2023.
 The improved return arrives after House Bill 231 was passed in 2025, which increased the annual grocery tax credit to $155 for all individuals starting in the 2026 fiscal year. The law also provides taxpayers the option to take a $155 tax credit per person or receive a refund of up to $250 on grocery taxes paid if grocery expenses are itemized on tax returns.
 Recent efforts to remove taxes on groceries in the state entirely have failed to make it into law. House Bill 633 was introduced this year to remove the grocery tax credit and replace it with a repeal of sales tax on most food, with exceptions for restaurant sales and prepared foods. That bill was introduced, but failed to ever receive a hearing.
 A citizen-led ballot initiative brought forward for this year’s election also sought to repeal the state’s grocery tax credit and exempt groceries in a similar manner to the proposed legislation, but was ultimately withdrawn from consideration ahead of the signature collection deadline .
 According to AARP , just eight states continue to have some form of tax on groceries and only three states, including Idaho, tax groceries at the regular sales tax rate. In the case of the other two states, Hawaii provides a grocery tax credit tied to income while South Dakota provides no such credit or exemptions.
 Royce McCandless is the Statehouse reporter and covers Idaho politics. You can email him at rmccandless@idahopress.com .
